original_question: Consider the single-input time-optimal control system q˙ = f(q) + u g(q) on a 3-dimensional smooth manifold M, where f and g are a generic pair of C-infinity vector fields, the control u is any measurable function with |u| <= 1, and trajectories are required to connect fixed endpoints in minimum time. Must every time-optimal trajectory for such a generic 3-dimensional system be piecewise smooth, meaning smooth except at finitely many switching points where the optimal control changes its regime?
target_in_paper: Section I, part A ("Singularities of time-optimal trajectories"): the open question for a generic pair (f,g) in dimension 3 asking whether time-optimal trajectories are piecewise smooth, with the draft matching most closely the weaker formulation explicitly stated there, namely whether every individual time-optimal trajectory has finitely many switching points.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the single-input control-affine system qdot = f(q) + u g(q), the 3-dimensional smooth-manifold setting, the C-infinity genericity of the pair (f,g), the measurable bounded control condition |u| <= 1, and the intended regularity issue: whether time-optimal trajectories have only finitely many switching points, i.e. are piecewise smooth.
missing_details: The paper first formulates the question for a generic pair (f,g) on an n-dimensional manifold and then says that the open case of primary interest is n = 3; your draft starts directly in dimension 3 and omits that framing.

Agrachev defines a switching point as a point where the admissible trajectory is not smooth; your gloss 'where the optimal control changes its regime' is close in spirit but is not the paper's exact definition.

The paper introduces a stronger local-uniform formulation via sw(q): the minimal k such that any time-optimal trajectory contained in a sufficiently small neighborhood of q has at most k switching points; sw(q) is set to infinity if every neighborhood of q contains a time-optimal trajectory with infinitely many switching points.

Your draft does not distinguish the stronger local question sw(q) < infinity for every q in M from the weaker trajectorywise question that each individual time-optimal trajectory has finitely many switching points.

The nearby context records partial 3-dimensional results that locate the remaining difficulty: sw(q) = 2 outside a 2-dimensional Whitney stratified subset of M, and sw(q) <= 4 outside a 1-dimensional Whitney stratified subset.
The paper explicitly says admissible trajectories are Lipschitz curves in M; that regularity assumption is implicit rather than stated in your draft.
The paper's wording is 'with fixed endpoint'; your draft says trajectories connect fixed endpoints. This is close, but not the exact phrasing used in the paper.

No ambient field/ring, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency conditions are relevant here; the important omitted quantifier structure is the local-in-q quantifier in the sw(q) formulation versus the per-trajectory quantifier in the weaker formulation.
refined_question: Let M be a 3-dimensional smooth manifold, and let (f,g) be a C-infinity-generic pair of smooth vector fields on M. For the time-optimal control problem qdot = f(q) + u g(q), with measurable controls satisfying |u| <= 1 and Lipschitz admissible trajectories, is every time-optimal trajectory piecewise smooth; equivalently in the paper's terminology, does every individual time-optimal trajectory have only finitely many switching points, where a switching point is a point at which the trajectory is not smooth?
justification: This draft is targeting Section I.A, not another part of the paper. Agrachev first introduces the system qdot = f(q) + u g(q), |u| <= 1, and then asks for a generic pair (f,g): 'Optimal trajectories cannot be all smooth; are they piecewise smooth?' He immediately states that the interesting open case is n = 3, defines the stronger local quantity sw(q), and explains that even the weaker statement that any individual time-optimal trajectory has finitely many switching points is unknown. Since your draft asks whether every time-optimal trajectory is smooth except at finitely many switching points, it aligns most closely with that weaker trajectorywise formulation, while the paper-faithful context also requires noting the stronger nearby sw(q) formulation.
